added_lines: Mon - Wed. 9.00am - 12. 30pm Pope Pius XI introduced the feast of Christ the King in 1925. This was a period of great tension ands tress in Europe; many nations were still badly divided and people were living their lives in fear. Throughout Europe totalitarianism and fascism had taken hold and their encouragement for intolerance, racism and persecution brought su ffering and fear to many. In Russia communism had taken hold and restricted people's freedom in varied ways. The feast of Christ the King that for believers there is a real gospel value, an allegiance higher than any other, an allegiance which prompts us to question all the ideologies or loyalties that would claim us. Christ can only be truly called King as the cruci fied one. That the group gathered around him could truly be the children of the kingdom undermines our assumptions about who is worthy and who is to be excluded. None of those who jeer at him or reject him are placed outside his concern or shephe rding care. The promise to the good thief is a symb ol of Christ exercising his kingly power to deliver his people from those who would deprive them of their freedom - just as prime duty for a political king is to ensure the security of his people. The qualities central to the kingdom of Christ are Love, Peace, Justice and Forgiveness. The central proclamation of Christianity is the victory of the Love of God. What does it mean in today's world to talk about the reign of Christ, when so many ideologies and things seem to reign? Certainly, weapons seem to rule; power seems to rule at times; terrorism seems to rule in many areas; violence rules in other quarters. For some, economics with its twin advertising and marketing rules; for others an addiction may rule the roost. However, on days like today let us reflect on the question, who or what is my master?The Family of Parishes of: Ballincollig | Ballinora | Kilmurry | Ovens and Farran Scan for Colour Version Prayer for Vocations Loving God, at baptism you have gifted each of us with a call to serve you and all people in everything we do. On this final Sunday of the Church year, the feast of Christ the King, we learn most de finitely how our lives will be measured. They will be measured by the love we show. Mon - Wed. 9.00am - 12. 30pm “The celebration of the World Day of the Poor is meant to remind our communities that the poor are at the heart of all our pastoral activity.” Pope Leo IVX Pope Francis established World Day of the Poor as an annual observance in 2017. after the Year of Mercy, Pope Francis said he wanted to set aside a day so that, throughout the world, Christian communities could become even greater signs of Christ’s charity for those in need.

As the Church prepares to observe the Tenth World Day of the Poor on Sunday, 15 November 2026, Pope Le o XIV delivered a message focused on the theme: “The Lord is the refuge of the poor” (Psalm 14:6), and focuses on condemning social injustice, arrogant corruption, and the factors that deepen poverty.

In his message for the 10th World Day of the Poor, Pope Leo XIV contemplates God as “the refuge of the poor.” He encourages Christians to re- evaluate the importance of the poor in our lives and to reflect on our dedication to justice, solidarity, and human dignity.

The Pope warns that the cry of the poor is often silenced through “a multitude of increasingly subtle tactics,” while the digital world can worsen prejudice and reinforce indifference and that “the poor of our day are the forgoƩen and the marginalised: robbed not only of bread, but also of a voice and a face.” “The poor have no choice but to cry out to God,” he writes, adding that they entrust themselves to Him “certain that they will be heard because God is faithful and rich in mercy.” The Holy Father expresses hope that the Tenth World Day of the Poor will help Christians “rediscover the faces of so many brothers and sisters who seek refuge in God and long to feel at home in our communities.” talents in the service of our parish community.

Organised by Trócaire on behalf of the Irish Bishops’ Conference and in partnership with the Laudato S i’ Movement the confe rence promises inspiring speakers, practical workshops and opportunities to share ideas.
Participants will discover ways to put Laudato Si’ into practice through parish action, biodiversity initiatives, ecological spirituality and climate justice.
